title: Symmetric and Exterior Powers

The space $B(V) \cong V^* \otimes V^*$ of bilinear forms contains the symmetric and the alternating forms. This section carries out the analogous constructions for all tensor powers. Throughout, $V$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $k$, $n = \dim V$, and $d \ge 0$.

## <span class="num">9.10.1</span> The Symmetric Group Acting on Tensors

For $\sigma \in S_d$, the map $V^d \to V^{\otimes d}$, $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(d)}$, is multilinear, so it induces a linear map $V^{\otimes d} \to V^{\otimes d}$, written $\eta \mapsto \sigma \cdot \eta$: $$\sigma \cdot (v_1 \otimes v_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d) = v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(2)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(d)}.$$ The factor in position $i$ moves to position $\sigma(i)$. This is an action of $S_d$ on $V^{\otimes d}$ by linear maps (Definition [3.2.1](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#definition-3-2-1)). Indeed, for $\sigma, \tau \in S_d$, writing $w_i = v_{\tau^{-1}(i)}$, $$\begin{aligned}
\sigma \cdot \big(\tau \cdot (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d)\big) &= \sigma \cdot (w_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes w_d) = w_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes w_{\sigma^{-1}(d)} \\
&= v_{\tau^{-1}\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\tau^{-1}\sigma^{-1}(d)},
\end{aligned}$$ which is $(\sigma\tau) \cdot (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d)$ because $(\sigma\tau)^{-1} = \tau^{-1}\sigma^{-1}$. Both sides are linear, so $\sigma \cdot (\tau \cdot \eta) = (\sigma\tau) \cdot \eta$ for all $\eta$, and clearly $e \cdot \eta = \eta$. (The inverses make this a left action for our convention that $\sigma\tau$ applies $\tau$ first.)

:::definition{9.10.1} Symmetric and alternating multilinear maps
A multilinear map $m : V^d \to U$ (where $V^d = V \times \cdots \times V$) is ***symmetric*** if $$m(v_{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v_{\sigma(d)}) = m(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \qquad \text{for all } \sigma \in S_d \text{ and all } v_i \in V,$$ and ***alternating*** if $m(v_1, \ldots, v_d) = 0$ whenever $v_i = v_j$ for some $i \neq j$. For $U = k$, the alternating multilinear maps are the alternating forms of Definition [5.4.1](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#definition-5-4-1), and for $d = 2$ and $U = k$ the symmetric and alternating ones are the symmetric and alternating bilinear forms of Definition [9.1.2](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#definition-9-1-2).
:::

:::lemma{9.10.2} Alternating maps change sign
Let $m : V^d \to U$ be multilinear and alternating.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. Exchanging two of the arguments of $m$ changes the sign of its value.
2. $m(v_{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v_{\sigma(d)}) = \sgn(\sigma)\, m(v_1, \ldots, v_d)$ for every $\sigma \in S_d$.
3. $m(v_1, \ldots, v_d) = 0$ whenever $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ are linearly dependent.

Conversely, if $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, a multilinear map with property (i) is alternating.
:::

:::proof
For alternating multilinear forms, that is, for $U = k$, these are parts (a)–(c) of Lemma [5.4.2](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#lemma-5-4-2). Their proofs use only that the map is multilinear and alternating, never that its values are scalars, so they apply word for word to $m$. For instance, (i) comes from expanding $$0 = m(\ldots, x + y, \ldots, x + y, \ldots) = m(\ldots, x, \ldots, y, \ldots) + m(\ldots, y, \ldots, x, \ldots),$$ where the two terms with a repeated argument have been dropped. For the converse, if exchanging two arguments changes the sign, then a value with the same vector $x$ in two positions equals its own negative, so twice it is $0$, and it is $0$ when $2 \neq 0$ in $k$.
:::

## <span class="num">9.10.2</span> Symmetric and Exterior Powers as Quotients

Let $J_d(V) \subseteq V^{\otimes d}$ be the subspace spanned by the tensors $\eta - \sigma \cdot \eta$ for $\eta \in V^{\otimes d}$ and $\sigma \in S_d$, and let $I_d(V) \subseteq V^{\otimes d}$ be the subspace spanned by the pure tensors $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$ with $v_i = v_j$ for some $i \neq j$. For $d \le 1$ both are zero.

:::definition{9.10.3} Symmetric power
The $d$th ***symmetric power*** of $V$ is the quotient space $$\Sym^d V = V^{\otimes d} / J_d(V).$$ The class of $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$ is written $v_1 v_2 \cdots v_d$.
:::

:::definition{9.10.4} Exterior power
The $d$th ***exterior power*** of $V$ is the quotient space $$\textstyle\bigwedge^d V = V^{\otimes d} / I_d(V).$$ The class of $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$ is written $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d$ and called a ***wedge product***.
:::

In $\Sym^d V$ the factors of a product $v_1 \cdots v_d$ may be permuted freely, since $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d - \sigma \cdot (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d)$ lies in $J_d(V)$. In $\bigwedge^d V$ a wedge product with a repeated factor is zero. Since $$v \otimes w + w \otimes v = (v + w) \otimes (v + w) - v \otimes v - w \otimes w \in I_2(V),$$ we get $v \wedge w = -w \wedge v$; the same computation in any two positions shows that exchanging two factors of a wedge product changes its sign. For small $d$, $\Sym^0 V = \bigwedge^0 V = k$ and $\Sym^1 V = \bigwedge^1 V = V$.

:::proposition{9.10.5} Universal properties
<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. The map $V^d \to \Sym^d V$, $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto v_1 \cdots v_d$, is multilinear and symmetric. For every symmetric multilinear map $m : V^d \to U$ there is a unique linear map $\tilde{m} : \Sym^d V \to U$ with $\tilde{m}(v_1 \cdots v_d) = m(v_1, \ldots, v_d)$.
2. The map $V^d \to \bigwedge^d V$, $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d$, is multilinear and alternating. For every alternating multilinear map $m : V^d \to U$ there is a unique linear map $\tilde{m} : \bigwedge^d V \to U$ with $\tilde{m}(v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d) = m(v_1, \ldots, v_d)$.

Consequently $\Hom(\Sym^d V, U)$ is isomorphic to the space of symmetric multilinear maps $V^d \to U$, and $\Hom(\bigwedge^d V, U)$ to the space of alternating multilinear maps $V^d \to U$.
:::

:::proof
The two maps are the composites of $\mu : V^d \to V^{\otimes d}$ with the quotient maps, so they are multilinear. The first is symmetric because $v_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma(d)} = \sigma^{-1} \cdot (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d)$ has the same class modulo $J_d(V)$ as $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$; the second is alternating by the definition of $I_d(V)$.

(i) Given $m$, let $\hat{m} : V^{\otimes d} \to U$ be the linear map with $\hat{m}(v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d) = m(v_1, \ldots, v_d)$ (Theorem [9.9.2](/notes/math-55a/9-9-multilinear-maps-and-the-tensor-algebra#theorem-9-9-2)). For each $\sigma$, the linear map $\eta \mapsto \hat{m}(\eta) - \hat{m}(\sigma \cdot \eta)$ vanishes on pure tensors because $m$ is symmetric, so it vanishes identically. Hence $J_d(V) \subseteq \ker \hat{m}$, and $\hat{m}$ factors through the quotient $\Sym^d V$.

(ii) If $m$ is alternating, $\hat{m}$ vanishes on the spanning elements of $I_d(V)$, so it factors through $\bigwedge^d V$.

In both cases $\tilde{m}$ is unique because the classes of pure tensors span the quotient. The last statement follows as for $V \otimes W$: $m \mapsto \tilde{m}$ is a linear bijection, with inverse given by composing with the map $V^d \to \Sym^d V$ or $V^d \to \bigwedge^d V$.
:::

:::proposition{9.10.6} Induced maps
Let $\varphi : V \to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional spaces. There are unique linear maps $\Sym^d \varphi : \Sym^d V \to \Sym^d W$ and $\bigwedge^d \varphi : \bigwedge^d V \to \bigwedge^d W$ with $$\begin{gathered}
\Sym^d \varphi\,(v_1 \cdots v_d) = \varphi(v_1) \cdots \varphi(v_d), \\
\textstyle\bigwedge^d \varphi\,(v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d) = \varphi(v_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge \varphi(v_d).
\end{gathered}$$ They satisfy $\bigwedge^d(\psi \circ \varphi) = \bigwedge^d \psi \circ \bigwedge^d \varphi$ and $\bigwedge^d(\id_V) = \id$, and likewise for $\Sym^d$.
:::

:::proof
The map $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto \varphi(v_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge \varphi(v_d)$ is multilinear, and alternating because $v_i = v_j$ implies $\varphi(v_i) = \varphi(v_j)$. Proposition [9.10.5](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-5) gives $\bigwedge^d \varphi$. Both sides of each identity are linear and agree on wedge products, which span. The case of $\Sym^d$ is the same.
:::

These induced maps are what make it possible to form the symmetric and exterior powers of a representation, a notion defined in Chapter 13 (Definition [13.1.1](/notes/math-55a/13-1-representations-and-subrepresentations#definition-13-1-1)).

## <span class="num">9.10.3</span> Bases and Dimensions

Fix a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ of $V$. For a $d$-tuple $J = (j_1, \ldots, j_d)$ of indices in $\{1, \ldots, n\}$, write $$t_J = e_{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes e_{j_d};$$ by Theorem [9.9.2](/notes/math-55a/9-9-multilinear-maps-and-the-tensor-algebra#theorem-9-9-2), these $n^d$ tensors form a basis of $V^{\otimes d}$. For $\sigma \in S_d$ we have $\sigma \cdot t_J = t_{\sigma J}$, where $\sigma J = (j_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, j_{\sigma^{-1}(d)})$ is $J$ with its entries rearranged.

:::proposition{9.10.7} Basis of $\Sym^d V$
For $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ with integers $a_i \ge 0$ and $a_1 + \cdots + a_n = d$, let $$e^a = e_1^{a_1} e_2^{a_2} \cdots e_n^{a_n} \in \Sym^d V$$ be the product of $a_1$ copies of $e_1$, $a_2$ copies of $e_2$, and so on. These monomials form a basis of $\Sym^d V$, and $$\dim \Sym^d V = \binom{n + d - 1}{d}.$$
:::

:::proof
*Spanning.* The classes of the $t_J$ span $\Sym^d V$. The class of $t_J$ is $e_{j_1} \cdots e_{j_d}$; since its factors may be permuted, it equals $e^{a(J)}$, where $a(J)_i$ is the number of entries of $J$ equal to $i$.

*Independence.* Let $E$ be a vector space with a basis $(\varepsilon_a)$ indexed by the exponent vectors $a$ of total $d$, and let $c : V^{\otimes d} \to E$ be the linear map with $c(t_J) = \varepsilon_{a(J)}$. Rearranging the entries of $J$ does not change $a(J)$, so $c(t_J - \sigma \cdot t_J) = 0$ for all $J$ and $\sigma$. Since the $t_J$ span $V^{\otimes d}$ and $\eta \mapsto \eta - \sigma \cdot \eta$ is linear, $c$ vanishes on $J_d(V)$, so it induces a linear map $\bar{c} : \Sym^d V \to E$ with $\bar{c}(e^a) = \varepsilon_a$. The $\varepsilon_a$ are linearly independent, hence so are the $e^a$.

*Counting.* Exponent vectors correspond to arrangements of $d$ stars and $n - 1$ bars in a row ($a_i$ is the number of stars between the $(i-1)$st and the $i$th bar), and there are $\binom{n + d - 1}{d}$ such arrangements.
:::

:::proposition{9.10.8} Basis of $\bigwedge^d V$
For an increasing tuple $I = (i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_d)$, write $e_I = e_{i_1} \wedge e_{i_2} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{i_d}$. These $\binom{n}{d}$ elements form a basis of $\bigwedge^d V$, so $$\dim \textstyle\bigwedge^d V = \dbinom{n}{d}.$$ In particular $\bigwedge^d V = 0$ for $d > n$.
:::

:::proof
Let $q : V^{\otimes d} \to \bigwedge^d V$ be the quotient map. Lemma [9.10.2](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#lemma-9-10-2)(ii), applied to the alternating map $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d$, gives $$q\big(\sigma \cdot (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d)\big) = v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \wedge \cdots \wedge v_{\sigma^{-1}(d)} = \sgn(\sigma^{-1})\, v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d,$$ and $\sgn(\sigma^{-1}) = \sgn(\sigma)$; by linearity, $q(\sigma \cdot \eta) = \sgn(\sigma)\, q(\eta)$ for all $\eta \in V^{\otimes d}$.

*Spanning.* The classes $q(t_J)$ span $\bigwedge^d V$. If $J$ has a repeated entry, $q(t_J) = 0$. If the entries of $J$ are distinct, let $I$ be the increasing tuple with the same entries; there is a unique $\rho_J \in S_d$ with $J = \rho_J I$, that is, $t_J = \rho_J \cdot t_I$, and then $q(t_J) = \sgn(\rho_J)\, e_I$. Hence the $e_I$ span.

*Independence.* Let $E$ be a vector space with a basis $(\varepsilon_I)$ indexed by the increasing $d$-tuples, and let $c : V^{\otimes d} \to E$ be the linear map with $c(t_J) = 0$ if $J$ has a repeated entry and $c(t_J) = \sgn(\rho_J)\, \varepsilon_I$ otherwise (with $I$ and $\rho_J$ as above). We show that $c$ vanishes on $I_d(V)$. Let $x = v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$ with $v_a = v_b$ for some $a < b$, let $\tau = (a\ b)$, and write $v_l = \sum_j x_{lj} e_j$. Expanding, $$x = \sum_J x_J\, t_J, \qquad x_J = x_{1 j_1} x_{2 j_2} \cdots x_{d j_d},$$ and $x_{\tau J} = x_J$ because $v_a = v_b$ (the tuple $\tau J$ is $J$ with its $a$th and $b$th entries exchanged). The terms with $j_a = j_b$ have $c(t_J) = 0$. The remaining tuples come in pairs $\{J, \tau J\}$ with $J \neq \tau J$, and $c(t_{\tau J}) = -c(t_J)$: either both tuples have a repeated entry, or $t_{\tau J} = \tau \cdot t_J = (\tau\rho_J) \cdot t_I$, so that $\rho_{\tau J} = \tau\rho_J$ and $\sgn(\rho_{\tau J}) = -\sgn(\rho_J)$. So the contributions of each pair cancel, and $c(x) = 0$. Thus $I_d(V) \subseteq \ker c$, and $c$ induces a linear map $\bar{c} : \bigwedge^d V \to E$ with $\bar{c}(e_I) = c(t_I) = \varepsilon_I$. The $\varepsilon_I$ are independent, hence so are the $e_I$.

If $d > n$ there are no increasing $d$-tuples, so $\bigwedge^d V = 0$.
:::

:::corollary{9.10.9} The top exterior power
If $\dim V = n$, then $\bigwedge^n V$ is one-dimensional, and for every basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ of $V$ the element $e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$ is a basis of $\bigwedge^n V$.
:::

The line $\bigwedge^n V$ is called the ***determinant line*** of $V$; Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3) below explains the name.

:::note
Compare the three dimension formulas, for $\dim V = n$:

- $\dim V^{\otimes d} = n^d$, the number of ordered $d$-tuples of indices;
- $\dim \Sym^d V = \binom{n+d-1}{d}$, the number of multisets of size $d$ from $n$ indices;
- $\dim \bigwedge^d V = \binom{n}{d}$, the number of subsets of size $d$ of $n$ indices.

Tensor powers remember the order of the factors; symmetric powers allow repeated factors and forget their order; exterior powers forbid repeated factors and remember their order only up to sign.
:::

:::proposition{9.10.10} Wedge products detect linear independence
Vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_d \in V$ are linearly independent if and only if $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d \neq 0$ in $\bigwedge^d V$.
:::

:::proof
If the $v_i$ are dependent, $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d = 0$ by Lemma [9.10.2](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#lemma-9-10-2)(iii), applied to the alternating map $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d$. If they are independent, extend them to a basis $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ of $V$. Then $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d$ is the basis element $e_I$, $I = (1, \ldots, d)$, of Proposition [9.10.8](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-8) for this basis, so it is nonzero.
:::

## <span class="num">9.10.4</span> Symmetric and Alternating Tensors

Many books define $\Sym^d V$ and $\bigwedge^d V$ as subspaces of $V^{\otimes d}$. When $d!$ is invertible in $k$, the subspaces are isomorphic to our quotients.

:::definition{9.10.11} Symmetric and alternating tensors
A tensor $\eta \in V^{\otimes d}$ is ***symmetric*** if $\sigma \cdot \eta = \eta$ for all $\sigma \in S_d$, and ***alternating*** if $\sigma \cdot \eta = \sgn(\sigma)\, \eta$ for all $\sigma \in S_d$. They form subspaces $\mcS^d(V)$ and $\mcA^d(V)$ of $V^{\otimes d}$.
:::

:::proposition{9.10.12} Tensor models when $d!$ is invertible
Suppose $d! \neq 0$ in $k$ (for instance, $\operatorname{char} k = 0$). Define linear maps $P_\mcS, P_\mcA : V^{\otimes d} \to V^{\otimes d}$ by $$P_\mcS(\eta) = \frac{1}{d!} \sum_{\sigma \in S_d} \sigma \cdot \eta, \qquad P_\mcA(\eta) = \frac{1}{d!} \sum_{\sigma \in S_d} \sgn(\sigma)\, \sigma \cdot \eta.$$ Then $P_\mcS$ is a projection onto $\mcS^d(V)$ with kernel $J_d(V)$, and $P_\mcA$ is a projection onto $\mcA^d(V)$ with kernel $I_d(V)$. Consequently $$V^{\otimes d} = \mcS^d(V) \oplus J_d(V) = \mcA^d(V) \oplus I_d(V),$$ and the quotient maps restrict to isomorphisms $\mcS^d(V) \to \Sym^d V$ and $\mcA^d(V) \to \bigwedge^d V$, whose inverses are $$\begin{gathered}
v_1 \cdots v_d \mapsto \frac{1}{d!} \sum_{\sigma \in S_d} v_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma(d)}, \\
v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d \mapsto \frac{1}{d!} \sum_{\sigma \in S_d} \sgn(\sigma)\, v_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma(d)}.
\end{gathered}$$
:::

:::proof
We treat $P_\mcA$; the argument for $P_\mcS$ is the same with the signs omitted. For $\tau \in S_d$, substituting $\rho = \tau\sigma$ and using $\sgn(\sigma) = \sgn(\tau)\sgn(\rho)$, $$\tau \cdot P_\mcA(\eta) = \frac{1}{d!} \sum_{\sigma} \sgn(\sigma)\, (\tau\sigma) \cdot \eta = \sgn(\tau)\, P_\mcA(\eta),$$ so the image of $P_\mcA$ lies in $\mcA^d(V)$. If $\eta \in \mcA^d(V)$, each term $\sgn(\sigma)\, \sigma \cdot \eta$ equals $\sgn(\sigma)^2 \eta = \eta$, so $P_\mcA(\eta) = \eta$. Hence $P_\mcA$ is a projection onto $\mcA^d(V)$, and $V^{\otimes d} = \mcA^d(V) \oplus \ker P_\mcA$.

Let $q : V^{\otimes d} \to \bigwedge^d V$ be the quotient map. As in the proof of Proposition [9.10.8](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-8), $q(\sigma \cdot \eta) = \sgn(\sigma)\, q(\eta)$, so $q(P_\mcA(\eta)) = \frac{1}{d!} \sum_\sigma \sgn(\sigma)^2 q(\eta) = q(\eta)$; that is, $\eta - P_\mcA(\eta) \in I_d(V)$ for every $\eta$. If $P_\mcA(\eta) = 0$, this says $\eta \in I_d(V)$. Conversely, let $x = v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$ with $v_a = v_b$ for some $a \neq b$, and let $\tau = (a\ b)$. Then $\tau \cdot x = x$, and substituting $\rho = \sigma\tau$ gives $P_\mcA(\tau \cdot x) = \sgn(\tau) P_\mcA(x)$, so $P_\mcA(x) = -P_\mcA(x)$. As $d \ge 2$, $2$ divides $d!$, so $2 \neq 0$ in $k$ and $P_\mcA(x) = 0$. Hence $\ker P_\mcA = I_d(V) = \ker q$. It follows that $q$ restricts to an isomorphism $\mcA^d(V) \to \bigwedge^d V$, with inverse $q(\eta) \mapsto P_\mcA(\eta)$. For $\eta = v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_d$ this inverse gives $\frac{1}{d!} \sum_\sigma \sgn(\sigma)\, v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(d)}$, which is the stated formula after replacing $\sigma$ by $\sigma^{-1}$.

For $P_\mcS$, the identity $\eta - P_\mcS(\eta) = \frac{1}{d!} \sum_\sigma (\eta - \sigma \cdot \eta)$ shows $\ker P_\mcS \subseteq J_d(V)$, and $P_\mcS(\sigma \cdot \eta) = P_\mcS(\eta)$ shows $J_d(V) \subseteq \ker P_\mcS$.
:::

:::note
Under these isomorphisms $e_1 \wedge e_2 \in \bigwedge^2 V$ corresponds to the alternating tensor $\frac12 (e_1 \otimes e_2 - e_2 \otimes e_1)$. Some authors identify $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d$ with $\sum_\sigma \sgn(\sigma)\, v_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma(d)}$, without the factor $\frac{1}{d!}$; this rescales the identification by $d!$. When $d! = 0$ in $k$, the subspace models break down: Exercise [9.11.14](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#exercise-9-11-14)(1) shows that over a field of characteristic $2$, $\mcA^2(k^2)$ is three-dimensional, while $\bigwedge^2 k^2$ is one-dimensional. This is why we define $\Sym^d V$ and $\bigwedge^d V$ as quotients.
:::

:::corollary{9.10.13} Symmetric and alternating parts of $V \otimes V$
Suppose $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, and let $\tau : V \otimes V \to V \otimes V$ be the swap, $\tau(v \otimes w) = w \otimes v$. Then $$V \otimes V = \mcS^2(V) \oplus \mcA^2(V) \cong \Sym^2 V \oplus \textstyle\bigwedge^2 V,$$ where $\tau$ acts as $+1$ on $\mcS^2(V)$ and as $-1$ on $\mcA^2(V)$. Under the isomorphism $V^* \otimes V^* \cong B(V)$ of Proposition [9.8.13](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-13)(ii), $\mcS^2(V^*)$ corresponds to the symmetric bilinear forms and $\mcA^2(V^*)$ to the skew-symmetric ones. Hence $B(V)$ is the direct sum of the symmetric and the skew-symmetric forms, and $$(V \otimes V)^* \cong \Sym^2(V^*) \oplus \textstyle\bigwedge^2(V^*).$$
:::

:::proof
The swap is the action of the transposition in $S_2$, so $\mcS^2(V) = \ker(\tau - \id)$ and $\mcA^2(V) = \ker(\tau + \id)$. Since $\tau^2 = \id$, every $\eta$ is the sum $\frac12(\eta + \tau\eta) + \frac12(\eta - \tau\eta)$ of an element of $\mcS^2(V)$ and an element of $\mcA^2(V)$; and if $\eta$ lies in both, then $\eta = \tau\eta = -\eta$, so $\eta = 0$. This is also the case $d = 2$ of Proposition [9.10.12](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-12), which gives the isomorphisms with $\Sym^2 V$ and $\bigwedge^2 V$. Under Proposition [9.8.13](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-13)(ii), $\ell \otimes m$ corresponds to $b(v, w) = \ell(v) m(w)$ and $\tau(\ell \otimes m) = m \otimes \ell$ to $m(v)\ell(w) = b(w, v)$; by linearity, $\tau$ corresponds to $b \mapsto b'$ with $b'(v, w) = b(w, v)$, whose $\pm 1$-eigenspaces are the symmetric and the skew-symmetric forms. Finally $(V \otimes V)^* \cong V^* \otimes V^*$ by Proposition [9.8.13](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-13)(i), and we apply the first statement to $V^*$.
:::

## <span class="num">9.10.5</span> The Symmetric Algebra and Polynomials

The product of the tensor algebra descends to symmetric powers. For $a, b \ge 0$, the map $V^a \times V^b \to \Sym^{a+b} V$ given by $$(v_1, \ldots, v_a, w_1, \ldots, w_b) \mapsto v_1 \cdots v_a w_1 \cdots w_b$$ is multilinear and symmetric in the $v_i$ for fixed $w_j$, so by Proposition [9.10.5](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-5) it induces, for each fixed $(w_1, \ldots, w_b)$, a linear map $\Sym^a V \to \Sym^{a+b} V$. For a fixed $\eta \in \Sym^a V$, the image of $\eta$ is multilinear and symmetric in $(w_1, \ldots, w_b)$: this holds when $\eta = v_1 \cdots v_a$, and such elements span $\Sym^a V$. So it induces a linear map $\Sym^b V \to \Sym^{a+b} V$. The result is a bilinear product $\Sym^a V \times \Sym^b V \to \Sym^{a+b} V$ with $$(v_1 \cdots v_a)(w_1 \cdots w_b) = v_1 \cdots v_a w_1 \cdots w_b.$$

:::definition{9.10.14} Symmetric algebra
The ***symmetric algebra*** of $V$ is $$\Sym^\bullet V = \bigoplus_{d=0}^{\infty} \Sym^d V,$$ with the product that extends the products $\Sym^a V \times \Sym^b V \to \Sym^{a+b} V$ bilinearly.
:::

The ***polynomial ring*** $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ in $n$ variables is the vector space with basis the monomials $x^a = x_1^{a_1} \cdots x_n^{a_n}$, $a \in \ZZ_{\ge 0}^n$, with the multiplication $x^a x^b = x^{a+b}$ extended bilinearly; for $n = 1$ it is the ring $k[x]$. The ***homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$*** are the linear combinations of the $x^a$ with $a_1 + \cdots + a_n = d$.

:::theorem{9.10.15} The symmetric algebra is a polynomial ring
$\Sym^\bullet V$ is a commutative ring with identity $1 \in \Sym^0 V = k$, and its multiplication is $k$-bilinear. If $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is a basis of $V$, the linear map $$\Sym^\bullet V \to k[x_1, \ldots, x_n], \qquad e^a \mapsto x^a,$$ is an isomorphism of rings. In particular, $\Sym^d V$ is isomorphic to the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $n$ variables.
:::

:::proof
The product is bilinear by construction, so it distributes over addition. Associativity can be checked on products of vectors, where both sides are $v_1 \cdots v_a w_1 \cdots w_b u_1 \cdots u_c$; commutativity too, since $w_1 \cdots w_b v_1 \cdots v_a$ differs from $v_1 \cdots v_a w_1 \cdots w_b$ only by a permutation of the factors. The element $1 \in \Sym^0 V$ is an identity. By Proposition [9.10.7](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-7), the monomials $e^a$ (of all degrees) form a basis of $\Sym^\bullet V$, so the map $e^a \mapsto x^a$ is a linear isomorphism. It is multiplicative on basis elements, because $e^a e^b = e^{a+b}$ (rearrange the factors) and $x^a x^b = x^{a+b}$; both products are bilinear, so the map is multiplicative.
:::

:::note
$\Sym^\bullet V$ is the coordinate-free version of the polynomial ring: it depends only on $V$, and a choice of basis identifies it with $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$.
:::

The most natural instance is $V^*$. If $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is a basis of $V$ and $x_i = e_i^*$, then $x_i(v)$ is the $i$th coordinate of $v$, and a product of the $x_i$ should be a polynomial function of the coordinates. A function $f : V \to k$ is a ***homogeneous polynomial function of degree $d$*** if $f(\sum_i c_i e_i) = p(c_1, \ldots, c_n)$ for a homogeneous polynomial $p$ of degree $d$; a linear change of coordinates turns homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ into homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$, so this does not depend on the basis.

:::proposition{9.10.16} $\Sym^d(V^*)$ and polynomial functions
Let $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ be a basis of $V$ and $x_i = e_i^*$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. There is a unique linear map $P$ from $\Sym^d(V^*)$ to the space of functions $V \to k$ with $P(\ell_1 \cdots \ell_d)(v) = \ell_1(v) \cdots \ell_d(v)$.
2. $P$ sends the monomial $x^a \in \Sym^d(V^*)$ to the function $v \mapsto x_1(v)^{a_1} \cdots x_n(v)^{a_n}$. So the image of $P$ is the space of homogeneous polynomial functions of degree $d$ on $V$.
3. If $k$ is infinite, $P$ is injective, and so is the map it induces on $\Sym^\bullet(V^*) \cong k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Thus $\Sym^d(V^*)$ is identified with the homogeneous polynomial functions of degree $d$ on $V$, and $\Sym^\bullet(V^*)$ with the ring of polynomial functions on $V$, the variable $x_i$ being the $i$th coordinate function.
:::

:::proof
(i) The map $(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_d) \mapsto (v \mapsto \ell_1(v) \cdots \ell_d(v))$ is multilinear and symmetric, with values in the vector space of functions $V \to k$; apply Proposition [9.10.5](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-5). (ii) follows from (i).

(iii) Extend $P$ to $\Sym^\bullet(V^*)$ degree by degree. By Theorem [9.10.15](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#theorem-9-10-15), an element of $\Sym^\bullet(V^*)$ is a polynomial $p = \sum_a c_a x^a$, and $P$ sends it to the function $v \mapsto p(x_1(v), \ldots, x_n(v))$. So it suffices to show that a polynomial $p \in k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ that vanishes at every point of $k^n$ is zero. We use induction on $n$. For $n = 1$, a nonzero polynomial has at most $\deg p$ roots (Corollary [4.3.15](/notes/math-55a/4-3-polynomial-rings-and-field-extensions#corollary-4-3-15)), while $k$ is infinite. For $n > 1$, write $p = \sum_j p_j(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1})\, x_n^j$. For each point $c \in k^{n-1}$, the one-variable polynomial $\sum_j p_j(c)\, x_n^j$ vanishes on all of $k$, so every $p_j(c) = 0$. Thus each $p_j$ vanishes on $k^{n-1}$, and $p_j = 0$ by induction.
:::

:::note
When $k$ is finite, $P$ need not be injective. Over $\FF_2$, the monomials $x_1^2 x_2$ and $x_1 x_2^2$ in $\Sym^3(V^*)$ define the same function, because $c^2 = c$ for every $c \in \FF_2$. So over finite fields $\Sym^d(V^*)$ consists of polynomials as algebraic expressions, and these carry more information than the functions they define.
:::

:::note
When $d! \neq 0$ in $k$, Propositions [9.10.12](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-12) and [9.9.6](/notes/math-55a/9-9-multilinear-maps-and-the-tensor-algebra#proposition-9-9-6) identify $\Sym^d(V^*)$ with the symmetric tensors in $(V^*)^{\otimes d}$, that is, with the symmetric $d$-linear forms on $V$. Following $\ell_1 \cdots \ell_d$ through these identifications gives the form $$\eta(v_1, \ldots, v_d) = \frac{1}{d!} \sum_{\sigma \in S_d} \ell_{\sigma(1)}(v_1) \cdots \ell_{\sigma(d)}(v_d),$$ and $\eta(v, \ldots, v) = \ell_1(v) \cdots \ell_d(v)$. So the polynomial function attached to a symmetric multilinear form $\eta$ is $v \mapsto \eta(v, \ldots, v)$. For $d = 2$ this is the passage from a symmetric bilinear form to its quadratic form (Section [9.6](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms)), and polarization (Proposition [9.6.2](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#proposition-9-6-2)) recovers the form from the function.
:::

## <span class="num">9.10.6</span> The Exterior Algebra

Exactly as for symmetric powers, the map $(v_1, \ldots, v_a, w_1, \ldots, w_b) \mapsto v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_a \wedge w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_b$ is multilinear and alternating in the $v_i$ for fixed $w_j$, and in the $w_j$ for fixed $v_i$. Applying Proposition [9.10.5](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-5) once in each variable gives a bilinear product $\bigwedge^a V \times \bigwedge^b V \to \bigwedge^{a+b} V$ with $$(v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_a) \wedge (w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_b) = v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_a \wedge w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_b.$$

:::definition{9.10.17} Exterior algebra
The ***exterior algebra*** (or ***Grassmann algebra***) of $V$ is $$\textstyle\bigwedge^\bullet V = \displaystyle\bigoplus_{d=0}^{n} \textstyle\bigwedge^d V,$$ with the product $\wedge$ that extends the products $\bigwedge^a V \times \bigwedge^b V \to \bigwedge^{a+b} V$ bilinearly. (Since $\bigwedge^d V = 0$ for $d > n$, the sum stops at $n$.)
:::

:::proposition{9.10.18} Properties of the exterior algebra
Let $\dim V = n$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\bigwedge^\bullet V$ is a ring with identity $1 \in \bigwedge^0 V = k$, its multiplication is $k$-bilinear, and $\dim \bigwedge^\bullet V = 2^n$.
2. The product is ***graded-commutative***: for $\eta \in \bigwedge^a V$ and $\theta \in \bigwedge^b V$, $$\theta \wedge \eta = (-1)^{ab}\, \eta \wedge \theta.$$
:::

:::proof
(i) Distributivity holds because the product is bilinear, and associativity and the identity can be checked on wedge products of vectors, where the product is concatenation. By Proposition [9.10.8](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-8), $\dim \bigwedge^\bullet V = \sum_{d=0}^{n} \binom{n}{d} = (1 + 1)^n = 2^n$.

(ii) Both sides are bilinear in $(\eta, \theta)$, so it suffices to take $\eta = v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_a$ and $\theta = w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_b$. Starting from $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_a \wedge w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_b$, move $v_a$ to the right past the $b$ factors $w_1, \ldots, w_b$, then $v_{a-1}$, and so on. This reaches $w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_b \wedge v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_a$ after $ab$ exchanges of adjacent factors, each of which changes the sign (Lemma [9.10.2](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#lemma-9-10-2)(i)).
:::

## <span class="num">9.10.7</span> Operators on Tensor, Symmetric, and Exterior Powers

For a diagonalizable operator, the induced operators on tensor, symmetric and exterior powers are easy to describe; this is what Chapter 13 uses to compute the characters of $\Sym^2 V$ and $\bigwedge^2 V$ (Definition [13.4.1](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#definition-13-4-1)).

:::proposition{9.10.19} Eigenvalues on tensor, symmetric, and exterior powers
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$, and suppose $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is a basis of $V$ with $\varphi(e_i) = \lambda_i e_i$. With the notation of Propositions [9.10.7](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-7) and [9.10.8](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-8):

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\varphi^{\otimes d}(t_J) = \lambda_{j_1} \cdots \lambda_{j_d}\, t_J$;
2. $\Sym^d \varphi\,(e^a) = \lambda_1^{a_1} \cdots \lambda_n^{a_n}\, e^a$;
3. $\bigwedge^d \varphi\,(e_I) = \lambda_{i_1} \cdots \lambda_{i_d}\, e_I$.

In particular $\varphi^{\otimes d}$, $\Sym^d \varphi$ and $\bigwedge^d \varphi$ are diagonalizable, and $$\begin{gathered}
\Tr(\varphi^{\otimes d}) = (\Tr \varphi)^d, \\
\Tr\big(\Sym^d \varphi\big) = \sum_{i_1 \le \cdots \le i_d} \lambda_{i_1} \cdots \lambda_{i_d}, \qquad \Tr\big(\textstyle\bigwedge^d \varphi\big) = \displaystyle\sum_{i_1 < \cdots < i_d} \lambda_{i_1} \cdots \lambda_{i_d}.
\end{gathered}$$ If $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, then $$\begin{gathered}
\Tr\big(\Sym^2 \varphi\big) = \tfrac12\big((\Tr \varphi)^2 + \Tr(\varphi^2)\big), \\
\Tr\big(\textstyle\bigwedge^2 \varphi\big) = \tfrac12\big((\Tr \varphi)^2 - \Tr(\varphi^2)\big).
\end{gathered}$$
:::

:::proof
By the definitions of the induced maps, $\bigwedge^d \varphi\,(e_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{i_d}) = \lambda_{i_1} e_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \lambda_{i_d} e_{i_d} = \lambda_{i_1} \cdots \lambda_{i_d}\, e_I$, and (i) and (ii) are the same computation. So each of the three bases consists of eigenvectors, and each trace is the sum of the eigenvalues. The monomials $e^a$ correspond to the nondecreasing tuples $i_1 \le \cdots \le i_d$ (list each index $i$ exactly $a_i$ times), which gives the formula for $\Tr(\Sym^d \varphi)$; the sum over all $d$-tuples $J$ of $\lambda_{j_1} \cdots \lambda_{j_d}$ is $(\sum_i \lambda_i)^d$. For $d = 2$, $\Tr \varphi = \sum_i \lambda_i$ and $\Tr(\varphi^2) = \sum_i \lambda_i^2$, since $\varphi^2(e_i) = \lambda_i^2 e_i$. From $(\sum_i \lambda_i)^2 = \sum_i \lambda_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j} \lambda_i \lambda_j$ we get $\Tr(\bigwedge^2 \varphi) = \sum_{i<j} \lambda_i\lambda_j = \frac12((\Tr\varphi)^2 - \Tr(\varphi^2))$, and $\Tr(\Sym^2 \varphi) = \sum_{i<j} \lambda_i\lambda_j + \sum_i \lambda_i^2 = \frac12((\Tr\varphi)^2 + \Tr(\varphi^2))$.
:::
